title: Discovery vs Direct Instruction
author: Dylan Kane
summary: Dylan Kane, an eighth grade maths teacher, takes on the polarised argument between discovery learning and direct instruction. He argues that either approach taught poorly or imposed by administrators fails, that students need practice, and that they also need to believe in themselves as problem solvers. He treats the debate as a false dichotomy along a spectrum of guidance. His proposal is to divide standards into two types: core ideas students must retain for years, taught with a mix of inquiry and direct instruction, and lower-stakes topics that serve as playgrounds for inquiry. He closes by saying maths is taught to exercise thinking, not to pass tests.
points: Poor teaching or top-down imposition spoils both discovery learning and direct instruction.
Discovery needs follow-up practice to retain; direct instruction risks students believing knowledge comes only from the teacher.
Guided versus unguided instruction is a spectrum, so the debate is a false dichotomy.
Core standards should be secured efficiently, while lower-stakes standards are ideal for inquiry.
Maths is taught to build logical thinking and pattern analysis, not to get a test score or job.
quotes: Discovery learning taught poorly is definitely a bad thing. Discovery learning pushed onto teachers from the administration is also a bad thing.

Students need to believe in their efficacy as problem solvers. This is, I think the pitfall of direct instruction -- students believe that knowledge comes from the teacher, and if they haven't been taught it, they can't do it.
For my purposes I'm using direct instruction as shorthand for teaching methods on the more-guided end of the spectrum, not for 100% guided instruction.

Type one, students have to learn. I would advocate for a mix of inquiry, problem-based learning, and direct instruction -- giving students an opportunity to figure as much out for themselves as they can, but also using direct instruction to make sure all students -- especially those with lower skills -- can solve these questions efficiently and apply the concepts appropriately.
We teach math to exercise their brains, their ability to solve puzzles, to think logically, to apply rules and analyze patterns.
